newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: 1,300 Turkish Kurds resettle in Iraq, UN says.
newsitem.headline: 1,300 Turkish Kurds resettle in Iraq, UN says.

text.p: Some 1,300 Turkish Kurd refugees have apparently left a troubled camp of 15,000 in northern Iraq and resettled on the edge of the zone controlled by the Iraqi government, a United Nations refugee agency said on Tuesday.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees in January withdrew from Atrush camp, which Turkey says is a base for guerrillas of the independence-seeking Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), saying Kurdish rebels among the refugees were blocking its aid work.

The agency, which said it could only provide aid to the Kurds if they left Atrush, encouraged the refugees to come to two temporary transit sites -- Muqibla and Balkus -- set up to allow the refugees to decide their destination in smaller groups.
But it has now begun delivering aid to Kurds who have resettled in Ain Sufni, according to a spokesman.

"We received reports over the weekend that some 1,300 Kurdish refugees have left Atrush camp and settled in Ain Sufni, near the Iraqi government controlled area," UNHCR spokesman Kris Janowski told a news briefing in Geneva.
"We're not quite sure whether it is government-controlled. It is actually right on the edge," he added.
UNHCR in Dohuk had registered 1,319 Kurds in Ain Sufni, the spokesman said, adding: "The fact that they moved that way means they are not particularly inclined to move toward Turkey."
The refugee agency and World Food Programme were delivering food, water, medicine tents and kerosene to the newly displaced.

UNHCR pulled out of Atrush on January 21, acknowledging the presence of PKK rebels in the camp, to whom it refers as activists, after repeated calls from Turkey for the separation of rebels from refugees and the closure of the camp.

Atrush, 60 km (38 miles) from the Turkish border, was set up in 1994 for Kurds fleeing into northern Iraq from south-east Turkey, where villagers are caught in the middle of a dirty guerrilla war between Turkish troops and the PKK. More than 21,000 people have died in the 12-year-old conflict.
